content: I'll read the test image first to identify the visual symptoms.

The test image shows a field-wide view of tomato plants with patchy wilting — some plants appear collapsed/wilted while adjacent ones remain healthy. This scattered whole-plant wilting pattern is characteristic of a soil-borne wilt disease.

Key observations:
- Whole-plant wilting (not leaf spots or lesions)
- Patchy distribution across rows — some plants dead/wilted, others healthy
- Complete collapse of affected plants
- Field-scale view suggesting soil-borne pathogen

Top candidates: Bacterial_Wilt, Southern_Bacterial_Wilt, Verticillium_Wilt. Let me view a reference for Bacterial_Wilt.

The reference image for Bacterial_Wilt shows the classic "streaming test" — bacterial ooze draining from a stem cross-section in water — confirming this is a bacterial pathogen causing rapid vascular occlusion and whole-plant wilting.

**Comparison analysis:**
- The test image shows a tomato field with patchy, complete whole-plant collapse scattered among healthy plants — the hallmark of Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum)
- Bacterial wilt causes sudden, complete wilting because the bacteria multiply rapidly in the xylem, blocking water transport
- The uneven/patchy distribution across the field rows matches the soil-borne spread pattern of R. solanacearum
- Verticillium Wilt would show more gradual, one-sided/partial wilting with yellowing rather than sudden complete collapse
- Southern_Bacterial_Wilt is the same pathogen but the field presentation here matches the classic Bacterial_Wilt description
